events.promise: Once you configure your trial signup as a goal in Plausible, you stop watching a single signup number and start seeing which landing pages and sources actually drive those signups.
events.arc: Single email: name the blind spot (a signup count with no attribution), show the concrete first step (configure a signup goal, pageview goals need no code), say what the Goals section then reports (conversion rate, referrer sources, entry pages, top converting pages), and send the reader to the official goal-conversions guide to set it up or review it.

emails.job: Get the reader to open the official goal-conversions guide and set up or review a trial-signup goal.
emails.single_idea: A signup count tells you nothing about where signups come from; configuring your trial signup as a goal in Plausible turns it into a conversion you can trace back to its source and landing page.
emails.objection: Does setting up a signup goal mean touching my code?
must_not_say: any measured lift the reader will get, or Plausible's own 2.65%-to-4.80% / 84% homepage figures as a promise
any assumption about which analytics tool they use now (no 'unlike Google Analytics', no GA import as a presumption)
any assumption about their traffic volume or plan tier (no 10k-pageview framing)
any assumption about their privacy or compliance status (don't tell them they do or don't need consent banners)
a product-trial or signup ask — the only CTA is the goal-conversions guide
promising full trial-to-paid or payment-failure tracking — that is out of scope for this email

Plausible can only record a paid conversion if the owner sends it as a backend event, revenue attribution sits on the Business plan, and the ledger contains nothing about in-trial product usage or billing, so the measurement stops at.

The 2.65% to 4.80% lift (E11) came from Plausible editing its own homepage, not from installing Plausible; the product locates entry pages and drop-off steps and the owner still has to make the change and re-measure.
emails.felt_need: Free-trial signups do not convert to paid at a rate the owner considers acceptable, even after a signup surge.
emails.status_quo: They add free trials that require a payment method upfront to try to convert website visitors into paying customers.
emails.why_it_fails: A bare signup count carries no source or entry-page breakdown, so you can't tell whether a particular page or channel is doing the work or just happened to coincide with the number moving.
emails.mechanism: You set your trial signup as a goal — for a register or confirmation page that's a pageview goal, which needs no code changes because pageviews are collected automatically. Once the goal records its first conversion, the dashboard reports its conversion rate and the referrer sources and entry pages driving those conversions, plus the top pages people convert on.
emails.next_step_decision: How to set up or review their trial-signup goal and read what the dashboard reports about it.
emails.next_step_value: The guide walks through configuring a pageview or custom-event goal and shows that the Goals section reports conversion rate, referrer sources, entry pages driving conversions and top converting pages.
emails.next_step_limit: It shows how to set up and read a goal; it does not set it up for them, does not promise a particular conversion rate, and does not cover trial-to-paid or billing outcomes.

events.preview_text: Mark the signup as a goal in Plausible and trace each one to its source
events.body:
In Plausible, you can mark your trial signup as a goal and then see which pages and sources are actually producing it.

A signup count on its own carries no breakdown. The number rises and falls, but it can't tell you whether a particular landing page or channel did the work or just happened to move at the same time.

For a register or confirmation page, that's a pageview goal — **no code changes**, since Plausible collects pageviews automatically.

Once it records its first conversion, the Goals section reports that goal's conversion rate, the referrer sources and entry pages driving those conversions, and the top pages people convert on.

The official goal-conversions guide walks through setting one up — pageview or custom event — and reading what the dashboard shows about it. It's the concrete first step from one signup total to signups you can trace back.

events.message: Email 1, draft 1: "See what drives signups, no code needed"
events.subject: See what drives signups, no code needed
events.preview_text: A pageview goal can trace signups to their source if yours ends on a thank-you page.
events.body:
You can count your trial signups. Seeing which pages and sources produced them is a different question.

Turning a signup into a conversion you can trace usually sounds like a code job — a custom event snippet to add before you measure anything. For an owner who isn't shipping code this week, that stalls.

Plausible is privacy-friendly web analytics with two goal types. If your signup finishes on a register or thank-you page, a pageview goal covers it with **no code**, because once Plausible is running those pageviews are collected automatically.

That goal still reports the referrer sources and entry pages driving your signups, plus the top pages people convert on. The snippet is only needed for actions that don't land on their own page.

The official goal-conversions guide walks through both types — which one fits a page-based signup, and when a custom event is actually worth the code.

edits.problem: Nothing on the page ever says what Plausible is; a cold reader is handed a proper noun and never learns this is privacy-friendly web analytics, so all three readers could only guess at the category.
edits.fix: Name what Plausible is, in the company's own words (privacy-friendly web analytics), in the sentence that first introduces it, early enough to orient a stranger.

edits.line: In Plausible, you can mark your trial signup as a goal
edits.problem: The opening presupposes the reader already runs Plausible, which the campaign explicitly forbade presuming; every cold reader named this unspecified-tool assumption as the thing that would stop them clicking.
edits.fix: Frame the capability so a reader whose current tool is unknown sees that it applies to them, without asserting they already use or have installed Plausible.

edits.line: A signup count on its own carries no breakdown.
edits.problem: The limitation is stated generically and never connected to the concrete question the breakdown answers for this reader, so the guide reads as permission to read rather than a useful next step.
edits.fix: Tie the missing breakdown to the specific question it resolves — which page or channel actually did the work — using only the supplied source/entry-page attribution, without promising any lift figure.

edits.line: Once it records its first conversion, the Goals section reports that goal's conversion rate, the referrer sources and entry pages driving those conversions, and the top pages people convert on.
edits.problem: Four payoffs crammed into one sentence blunt the single promise the subject line made; readers flagged it as a feature pile-up.
edits.fix: Split the sentence or lead with the one payoff that matches the subject line so the core promise lands.

events.preview_text: Your signup total can't say; a goal in Plausible can
events.body:
Your trial signups rise and fall. Which page or which source produced them is a separate question your total can't answer.

Plausible is **privacy-friendly web analytics**. Set it up on your site and you can mark your trial signup as a goal — the kind of action goals exist for, alongside a newsletter signup or a completed checkout.

For a register or confirmation page, that's a pageview goal. Pageviews are collected automatically, so tracking one needs **no change to your site's code**.

Once the goal records its first conversion, the Goals section reports its conversion rate — and the referrer sources, entry pages and top converting pages behind it. That's which channel or page did the work, not just that the number moved.

The official goal-conversions guide walks through setting one up — pageview or custom event — and reading what the dashboard shows about it.
